items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
そば米雑炊は、そばの実を殻のままゆでて乾燥させた「そば米」を主役にした一椀。米粒ではなく蕎麦の実そのものを使うため、ゆでるとふっくらと四倍近くにふくらみ、噛むとぷちぷちとした食感と香ばしい風味が広がる。鶏肉やこんにゃく、にんじん、干ししいたけなどをだしでやわらかく煮込み、しょうゆやみりんで味を調えたところへそば米を加えて仕上げる。そば自体がたんぱく質やミネラル、食物繊維を豊富に含み、具だくさんの汁と合わさることで栄養バランスのとれた一品になっている。
## どう作るのか
たっぷりの水でそば米を10～15分ほどゆで、水洗いしてザルにあげておく。にぼしや干ししいたけの戻し汁でだしを取り、鶏肉、にんじん、こんにゃく、ちくわ、干ししいたけを加えて中火で煮込む。薄口しょうゆとみりんで味を調えたら、最後にゆでておいたそば米を加え、青ねぎを散らして仕上げる。そば米は主食を兼ねるため惜しみなくたっぷりと用意するのが、汁というより雑炊らしい満足感につながっている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
そば米雑炊が生まれた祖谷地方は山々に囲まれ、稲作に向かない土地だったとされる。源平合戦に敗れた平家の落人がこの地に逃れた際、米の代わりに栽培期間の短いそばを育てたことが定着のきっかけと伝わる。そばの実を粉にせず、そのまま塩ゆでして食べる工夫は、山あいの厳しい環境で限られた食材を余さず活かす知恵だったといえそうだ。正月にはこれへ山鳥を加え、ご馳走として振る舞うこともあったという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Sobagome zōsui centers on "sobagome" — whole buckwheat groats that are boiled in their husks and dried rather than milled into flour. Cooked, the groats swell to nearly four times their size, giving each spoonful a nutty flavor and a distinctive light snap. Chicken, konjac, carrot, and dried shiitake are simmered in dashi and seasoned with soy sauce and mirin before the groats are stirred in. Buckwheat itself is rich in protein, minerals, and fiber, so the dish, loaded with vegetables and meat, ends up well balanced nutritionally.
## How it's made
The groats are boiled for ten to fifteen minutes in plenty of water, then rinsed and drained. A dashi is made from dried sardines and the soaking liquid of dried shiitake, and chicken, carrot, konjac, fish cake, and shiitake are simmered in it over medium heat. Once seasoned with light soy sauce and mirin, the pre-boiled sobagome is added last, and the dish is finished with a scattering of scallions. The groats double as the starch of the meal, so they are used generously, giving the dish the heft of a porridge rather than a thin soup.
## Why it took this shape
The dish is said to have taken root in the Iya valley, a mountainous area poorly suited to rice cultivation. When Taira clan survivors reportedly fled there after their defeat in the Genpei War, they are said to have turned to buckwheat, which grows in a much shorter season than rice, in place of it. Boiling the whole groats rather than milling them into flour looks like a way of making full use of a limited harvest in a harsh mountain environment. At New Year's, the dish was reportedly enriched with wild fowl and served as a festive treat.

sources.title: そば米雑炊／そば米汁 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
酢と醤油で下味をつけたちりめんじゃこに、ちくわ、しいたけ、こんにゃく、ごぼうなどを細かく刻んで炊きたてのご飯に混ぜ込んだ、佐那河内村嵯峨地区に伝わる混ぜご飯。じゃこの塩気と酸味、根菜の歯ごたえが混ざり合い、おかずいらずでも満足できる素朴な味わいが特徴とされる。ちりめんは小松島市和田島町でとれたものを天日干しにしたものが使われることが多く、香ばしさと旨みが強い。すだちを添えて爽やかさを加えることもある。
## どう作るのか
先にご飯を炊いておき、酢と醤油で味をつけたちりめんと、だしやしょうゆ、みりんで煮詰めたこんにゃく、ごぼう、しいたけなどをよく混ぜ合わせる。具材を煮るだしには煮干しを使うことが多く、かえりちりめんの漬け汁に地元産のすだちを絞り入れて風味を足すこともある。手順は混ぜるだけとシンプルで、副菜を用意しなくても一品で満足できる作りになっている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
嵯峨地区では昔、用水路の手入れや草刈りを住民総出で行う「つじ仕事」の後や、農作業の合間にねぎらいとしていり飯が振る舞われていたと伝わる。混ぜるだけで手早く作れ、大人数分をまとめて用意しやすいことが、共同作業の合間の食事として選ばれた理由のようだ。100年以上前から受け継がれてきたとされ、村の集会でも振る舞われるなど、地域の結びつきとともに残ってきた料理といえる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Iri-meshi is a mixed rice dish from the Saga district of Sanagōchi village, made by folding vinegar- and soy-seasoned chirimen (dried baby sardines) together with finely chopped fish cake, shiitake, konjac, and burdock into freshly cooked rice. The salty, tangy sardines and the crunch of root vegetables combine for a simple flavor said to be satisfying enough on its own, without side dishes. The chirimen typically comes from Wadajima in Komatsushima, sun-dried for extra aroma and umami, and a squeeze of sudachi citrus is sometimes added for brightness.
## How it's made
Rice is cooked first. Chirimen seasoned with vinegar and soy sauce is mixed with konjac, burdock, and shiitake that have been simmered down in dashi, soy sauce, and mirin. Dried sardines are the usual base for that dashi, and some cooks add local sudachi juice to the sardines' soaking liquid for extra fragrance. The method is simple — everything is just mixed together — which is part of why the dish works as a one-bowl meal that needs no side dishes.
## Why it took this shape
In the Saga district, iri-meshi is said to have been served after "tsuji-shigoto," communal work parties that maintained irrigation channels and cleared grass, or during breaks in farm work, as a way of thanking the workers. Because it comes together quickly by mixing and can be prepared in large batches, it suited meals shared during breaks from group labor. Handed down for more than a century by some accounts, it was reportedly also served at village gatherings, a dish that has endured alongside the community ties that shaped it.

sources.title: いり飯 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
甘辛く煮た金時豆と、その時々の旬の食材を酢飯に混ぜ込んだ、彩り豊かな寿司。こんにゃくやにんじん、ごぼう、ちくわ、しらすや焼き魚などを合わせ、すだちや柚子酢などかんきつ系の酢で仕立てるのが徳島流とされる。ゆずの皮のせん切りやごまで香りを添えることもあり、見た目も華やかな一品になる。呼び名は地域によって「まぜくり」「五目ずし」「かきまぜ」などさまざまだという。
## どう作るのか
すだちや柚子酢を効かせた合わせ酢ですし飯を作り、だしと砂糖、しょうゆで煮含めたこんにゃく、ちくわ、にんじん、ごぼうなどを混ぜ込む。春はぜんまいやわらび、たけのこ、そらまめといった旬の山菜や野菜を加え、地域によっては干し大根や干しなすを入れることもある。県南部では金時豆の代わりに落花生を煮て使うこともあるといい、各家庭の味が出やすい料理となっている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
徳島はもともと稲作に向かない土地が多く、米の代わりにさまざまな具材をたっぷり加えてかさを増やしたことがこの寿司の始まりと伝わる。祭りや節句など祝い事の折に大量に作り、家族で食べるだけでなく客に振る舞ったり土産にしたりする習わしがあったという。陰暦十月の亥の日に食べるものは「いのこずし」と呼ばれ、升に八分目ほど盛って翌年の豊作を願う風習も残っているとされる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
This colorful sushi mixes sweet-savory simmered kintoki beans with whatever is in season into vinegared rice. Konjac, carrot, burdock, fish cake, whitebait, or grilled fish are typically added, and the vinegar is often citrus-based, made with sudachi or yuzu juice, which is said to be the Tokushima style. Some cooks add shredded yuzu peel or sesame for fragrance, making for a dish as visually vivid as it is flavorful. Depending on the area it is also known as "mazekuri," "gomoku-zushi," or "kakimaze."
## How it's made
Vinegared rice is made with a citrus-forward vinegar blend of sudachi or yuzu, then mixed with konjac, fish cake, carrot, and burdock simmered in dashi, sugar, and soy sauce. In spring, seasonal mountain vegetables such as osmund fern, bracken, bamboo shoots, or fava beans are folded in, and some regions add dried daikon or dried eggplant. In the south of the prefecture, peanuts are sometimes simmered in place of kintoki beans, which is part of why the dish varies so much from household to household.
## Why it took this shape
Much of Tokushima was reportedly poor land for growing rice, and this sushi is said to have begun as a way of bulking up rice with plenty of other ingredients. It was made in large batches for festivals and seasonal celebrations, eaten by the family but also, it's said, served to guests or given as gifts. A version eaten on the Day of the Boar in the tenth lunar month is called "inoko-zushi," and by one account it was piled eight-tenths full in a measuring box as a wish for a bountiful harvest the following year.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
餅の代わりに、大きくて硬い「岩豆腐（石豆腐）」を具に使う、三好市祖谷地方独特の雑煮。大豆をふんだんに使い、にがりを多めに加えてしっかり水切りすることで、縄で縛って持ち運べるほど硬い豆腐に仕上げる。いりこだしのつゆに煮しめた里芋を入れ、その上に岩豆腐を重ねて盛るのが特徴で、豆腐の重なる姿が武士が刀を打ち違える様子に似ていることが名の由来とされる。
## どう作るのか
いりこでだしを取り、しょうゆなどで味を調えてつゆを作る。里芋は八つ頭を使うことが多く、これを煮しめてつゆに数個入れ、その上に長方形に切った大きな岩豆腐を2枚のせて仕上げる。餅を焼いたり煮たりする一般的な雑煮とは違い、硬い豆腐をそのまま盛り付けるだけというシンプルな作りだが、豆腐自体の仕込みには手間と時間がかかるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
祖谷地方は米が育ちにくく、主食は麦やそばだったと伝わる。稲作に頼れない土地でたんぱく源として重宝されたのが、水分を抜いて硬く仕立てた岩豆腐だった。冷蔵庫のない時代、水気の少ない豆腐は日持ちがよく持ち運びもできたため、正月などのハレの日に欠かせない食材になったとされる。里芋には八つ頭のように一つの芋から多くの芽が出る種を選び、「芽出たい」にかけて祝いの席にふさわしい縁起物としたという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
In this version of zōni unique to the Iya region of Miyoshi, "iwa-dōfu" (rock tofu) — large, dense blocks of tofu — stands in for the rice cakes usually found in the dish. Made with plenty of soybeans, extra nigari coagulant, and thorough draining, it comes out firm enough to be tied with rope and carried. The broth, made with dried sardine dashi and simmered taro, is topped with slabs of this tofu, and the way the pieces stack is said to resemble swordsmen crossing blades — reportedly the origin of the dish's name, "uchigae," meaning "crossed strikes."
## How it's made
Dashi is drawn from dried sardines and seasoned with soy sauce to make the broth. Yatsugashira taro, a variety that produces many offshoots from one corm, is typically simmered and added a few pieces at a time, then topped with two large rectangular slabs of the rock tofu. Unlike ordinary zōni, where rice cakes are grilled or simmered, this dish is simply assembled with the firm tofu as is — though making the tofu itself is said to take considerable time and effort.
## Why it took this shape
Rice reportedly grew poorly in the Iya region, where wheat and buckwheat were the staple grains instead. In land unsuited to rice farming, this firm, moisture-drained tofu became a valued source of protein. Before refrigeration, its low moisture content meant it kept well and could be carried, which is said to be why it became essential for New Year's and other festive occasions. The taro variety chosen, which sprouts many buds from a single corm, was reportedly picked for its association with abundance, making it fitting for celebratory meals.

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
大根、にんじん、油揚げ、ごま、れんこん、干ししいたけ、こんにゃくなど七つの食材を三杯酢で和えた、さっぱりとした一皿。白ごまの香ばしさと酢の酸味、根菜の食感が重なり合い、甘い酢の味わいは子どもにも好まれたと伝わる。名前の由来は「七つの食材を使うから」とも、かつて具材に加えられていた野菜の粕漬け「奈良漬け」を「奈良和え」と呼んだことに由来するともいわれ、はっきりしないという。
## どう作るのか
野菜と油揚げを食べやすい大きさに切り、干ししいたけの戻し汁でやわらかく煮る。水気を切ったら、白ごま、酢、柚子酢、砂糖、しょうゆで作った合わせ酢に入れ、しばらくなじませて味をしみ込ませる。家庭では七つの食材にこだわらず、たけのこやきゅうり、みょうが、三つ葉、豆腐、昆布など、そのとき手元にある旬の野菜を使うのが一般的だという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
ならえは大化の改新の頃に食べられていた精進料理の一つだったと伝わり、法事や彼岸など仏事の席で供されてきた。肉や魚を使わず野菜と乾物だけで作れる精進料理としての性格が、仏事に結びついた理由のようだ。美馬町では祝い事の際に味噌汁やお平、白和えなどとともに供する風習もあったとされ、甘い酢の味は甘味の乏しかった時代、子どもたちの楽しみでもあったという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Narae is a refreshing salad of daikon, carrot, fried tofu, sesame, lotus root, dried shiitake, and konjac — traditionally seven ingredients — dressed in a three-part vinegar sauce. The nuttiness of white sesame, the tang of vinegar, and the crunch of root vegetables come together, and the dish's sweet vinegar flavor is said to have been especially popular with children. The name's origin is unclear: some say it comes from using seven ("nana") ingredients, others that it derives from "Nara-ae," an old term for pickled vegetables once included in the dish.
## How it's made
The vegetables and fried tofu are cut into bite-sized pieces and simmered until tender in the soaking liquid from dried shiitake. Once drained, they are tossed in a dressing of white sesame, vinegar, yuzu vinegar, sugar, and soy sauce and left to absorb the flavor. Households are not strict about the traditional seven ingredients; bamboo shoots, cucumber, myoga ginger, mitsuba, tofu, or kelp — whatever seasonal vegetables are on hand — are commonly substituted.
## Why it took this shape
Narae is said to date back to a shōjin-ryōri (Buddhist vegetarian) dish eaten around the time of the Taika Reform, and it has long been served at memorial services and equinox observances. Its character as a meat- and fish-free dish made from vegetables and dried goods appears to be why it became tied to Buddhist occasions. In the Mima area, it's reportedly also served at celebrations alongside miso soup and other dishes, and in an age when sweets were scarce, its sweet vinegar flavor was said to be a treat children looked forward to.

sources.title: ならえ うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
ゆべしは、ゆずの皮を細かく刻み、砂糖としょうゆでじっくり煮詰めて仕上げる甘辛い保存食。ゆずの苦みと酸味に砂糖のコクとしょうゆの塩気が溶け合い、噛むほどに皮のほろ苦さと柑橘の香りが広がる。那賀町相生地区をはじめとする那賀川上流や勝浦地方、上勝町では、地元産のゆずを使って各家庭で作られてきたとされる。そのままご飯のおかずにするほか、酒のつまみやお茶漬けの具材として楽しまれることもある。
## どう作るのか
ゆずの皮を細かく刻み、たっぷりの水を張った鍋に入れて水から煮る。沸騰したら水を替える作業を繰り返して苦みをやわらげ、砂糖としょうゆを加えて粘り気が出るまでじっくり煮詰める。皮は先に天日干しにして保存しておき、使う際にふやかしてから煮詰めることもあるという。手間と時間をかけて仕上げる分、日持ちのする常備菜になる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
那賀町一帯は降水量が多く、昼夜の寒暖差が大きいことからゆず栽培に適した土地とされ、良質なゆずが豊富に採れる。収穫の最盛期である11月ごろ、果汁を搾った後の皮を捨てずに活用しようとしたことが、ゆべしが生まれた理由のひとつと考えられる。砂糖が貴重だった時代には頻繁には作れなかったが、家庭で砂糖を使いやすくなった昭和30年代以降に広まり、秋から春にかけておかずが少ない時期の副菜として重宝されてきたとされる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Yubeshi is a sweet-savory preserve made by finely chopping yuzu peel and slowly simmering it down with sugar and soy sauce. The citrus's bitterness and tartness meet the richness of sugar and the saltiness of soy sauce, and each bite releases a mild bitterness from the peel along with a burst of citrus aroma. It's said to have been made in home kitchens across the upper Naka River area around Naka town's Aioi district, as well as Katsuura and Kamikatsu, using locally grown yuzu. It's eaten as a side dish with rice, but also as a snack with sake or mixed into ochazuke.
## How it's made
The chopped yuzu peel goes into a pot with plenty of water, starting from cold. The water is brought to a boil and changed several times to soften the bitterness, and then sugar and soy sauce are added and simmered slowly until the mixture turns sticky. The peel is sometimes sun-dried for storage first and rehydrated before simmering. The time and effort involved is what makes it keep well as a pantry staple.
## Why it took this shape
The Naka town area gets heavy rainfall and a wide swing between day and night temperatures, conditions said to suit yuzu cultivation, so good-quality fruit has long been plentiful there. Making the most of the peel left over after squeezing juice around the November harvest peak appears to be one reason yubeshi came about. Sugar was once too scarce for the dish to be made often, but it's said to have spread once sugar became more common in home kitchens from the 1950s on, valued as a side dish for the season from autumn to spring when other dishes were scarce.

sources.title: ゆべし うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
みそで味を調えた雑炊「おみいさん」は、里芋や大根、大根の葉をたっぷり加えて仕立てる素朴な一杯。みそのコクと根菜の甘み、いりこだしの旨みが溶け合い、体の温まるやさしい味わいになる。名前は、みそを昔「みい」と呼び、そこに尊敬の意を表す「お」と「さん」を添えたことに由来するとされる。豆腐やニラを加えるなど、決まった具材はなく各家庭で少しずつ違う顔を持つ。
## どう作るのか
里芋、大根、大根の葉を細かく切り、煮干しのだし汁に洗った米とともに入れて煮立たせる。沸騰したら弱火にし、みそを塊のまま鍋全体に散らして溶かしていく。30分ほど煮るとみそが溶けて米がやわらかくなるので、かき混ぜて蒸らせば完成。みそを入れたあとにかき混ぜると焦げやすいため、そのままにしておくのがコツだという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
米が育ちにくかった徳島では、米に大根や里芋をたっぷり加えてかさを増やす工夫が各地でされてきたと伝わる。おみいさんもその一つで、出荷できない小米や冷や飯、みそ汁の残りなど、無駄にできない食材を使い切るための日常料理として根づいたようだ。体を温める効果もあることから冬によく食べられたほか、体調がすぐれないときに家族が作る料理としても親しまれてきたという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Omiisan is a humble rice porridge seasoned with miso and loaded with taro, daikon, and daikon greens. The richness of the miso, the sweetness of the root vegetables, and the umami of dried-sardine dashi combine into a warming, comforting bowl. The name is said to come from an old word for miso, "mii," with the honorific prefix "o" and suffix "san" added on. There's no fixed ingredient list — tofu or garlic chives are sometimes added — so the dish looks a little different from one household to the next.
## How it's made
Taro, daikon, and daikon greens are finely chopped and brought to a boil in dashi made from dried sardines, together with washed rice. Once it boils, the heat is lowered and lumps of miso are scattered across the pot to dissolve. After about thirty minutes the miso has melted and the rice has softened; it's stirred and left to steam before serving. Stirring right after adding the miso is said to make it catch on the bottom of the pot, so it's left alone instead.
## Why it took this shape
In Tokushima, where rice was hard to grow, it's said that households across the region found ways to stretch rice by adding plenty of daikon and taro. Omiisan appears to be one such dish, taking root as an everyday way of using up small, unmarketable rice grains, leftover cold rice, or miso soup dregs rather than wasting them. Its warming quality made it a common winter dish, and it's also said to have been the meal a family would make for someone feeling unwell.

sources.title: おみいさん うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
「茶ごめ」は、煎ったそら豆とざらめ糖を米と一緒に炊き上げた、ほんのり甘いご飯。そら豆の香ばしさとざらめ糖のやさしい甘みがご飯全体に行き渡り、名前の通り茶色く色づいた見た目になる。かつては武家屋敷で食べられていたとされるが、その後は新しいそら豆が出回る時季に古い豆を使い切る目的で農家に広まったと伝わる。たくあんや梅干しなどの漬物や、お茶を添えて食べることもある。
## どう作るのか
そら豆はまず弱火でじっくりと煎り、茶褐色になったら湯に30分ほどつけてから沸騰させる。米とざらめ糖、そら豆のゆで汁を炊飯器に入れて炊き上げれば完成となる。そら豆を焦がさないよう弱火でじっくり加熱するのがポイントで、下ごしらえには時間がかかるものの、炊飯器まかせで仕上げられるため手順自体は難しくない。炊き上がったご飯にはたくあんや梅干しなどの漬物を添え、お茶とともに食べることもあるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
茶ごめは農作業の合間に食べられることが多く、ざらめ糖の甘みが疲れた体をいたわる役割を果たしていたとされる。米に別の食材を加えて量を増やす工夫が徳島の郷土料理に多く見られる中、茶ごめは新豆の収穫期に余った古いそら豆を無駄にしないための知恵として広まったと考えられる。地域によっては正月の行事食として供したり、法事で仏壇に供えたりする風習も残っているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Chagome is a subtly sweet rice dish made by cooking roasted fava beans and coarse sugar together with the rice. The nuttiness of the beans and the gentle sweetness of the sugar spread through every grain, giving the rice the brownish color that gives the dish its name ("tea rice"). It's said to have once been eaten in samurai households, later spreading to farming families as a way to use up last year's fava beans once the new crop came in. It's sometimes served with pickles like takuan or umeboshi, alongside a cup of tea.
## How it's made
The fava beans are first roasted slowly over low heat until browned, then soaked in hot water for about thirty minutes before being brought to a boil. Rice, coarse sugar, and the beans' cooking liquid go into the rice cooker together. Roasting the beans slowly without scorching them is the key step; the prep takes some time, but the process itself is simple and approachable.
## Why it took this shape
Chagome was commonly eaten during breaks in farm work, and the sweetness of the coarse sugar is said to have been a welcome comfort for tired bodies. Stretching rice with other ingredients shows up often in Tokushima's home cooking, and chagome looks like it grew out of a similar impulse — a way to use up leftover fava beans from the previous year before the new harvest came in, rather than waste them. In some areas it's reportedly still served as a New Year's dish or offered at the household altar during memorial services.

sources.title: 茶ごめ うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
でんぶは、下ゆでした金時豆や黒豆を大根やごぼうなどの根菜と一緒に煮込み、しょうゆと砂糖で甘辛く仕上げた、五目豆に似た一品。「おでんぶ」「れんぶ」などとも呼ばれる。豆のほっくりとした食感と根菜の歯ごたえ、甘辛いたれが絡み合い、豆にはたんぱく質、根菜には食物繊維が豊富に含まれ栄養価も高い。家庭によっては梅干しを加えてさっぱりと仕上げることもあるという。
## どう作るのか
金時豆は下ゆでの際にゆで汁から出すとしわが寄ってしまうため、差し水をしながらゆでるのがコツとされる。にんじん、大根、ごぼうに加え、ちくわやれんこん、油揚げ、昆布、高野豆腐などその家にある食材を1cm角ほどに切りそろえ、煮干しのだし、しょうゆ、砂糖、料理酒でじっくり煮含める。使う具材に決まりはなく、各家庭で少しずつ違う仕上がりになるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
でんぶは正月の白みそ仕立ての雑煮や煮しめとともに供される祝い事の料理として広まったとされる。豆が主役であることから「まめに働いて暮らせるように」との願いが込められているといい、高価な食材を使わない構成は、貧しい家庭でも正月を祝えるようにという工夫から生まれたと伝わる。正月には金時豆の代わりに黒豆を使うこともあるという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Denbu simmers pre-boiled kintoki or black beans together with root vegetables like daikon and burdock, seasoned sweet and savory with soy sauce and sugar — a dish resembling gomoku-mame. It also goes by names like "odenbu" or "renbu." The mealy texture of the beans, the crunch of the root vegetables, and the sweet-savory glaze combine into a dish rich in both protein from the beans and fiber from the vegetables. Some households add umeboshi for a touch of tartness.
## How it's made
When par-boiling kintoki beans, adding cold water partway through the boil is said to be the trick to keeping the skins from wrinkling. Carrot, daikon, and burdock are joined by whatever else a household has on hand — fish cake, lotus root, fried tofu, kelp, or freeze-dried tofu — all cut into roughly one-centimeter cubes, then slowly simmered in dried-sardine dashi, soy sauce, sugar, and cooking sake. There's no fixed set of ingredients, so the result varies a little from home to home.
## Why it took this shape
Denbu is said to have spread as a festive dish served alongside white-miso zōni and simmered vegetables at New Year's. Because beans are the centerpiece, the dish is said to carry a wish tied to the word "mame" (beans), which also means diligence — a hope for a hardworking, steady life. Its avoidance of costly ingredients is said to reflect an effort to let even poorer households celebrate the New Year properly, and black beans are sometimes used in place of kintoki beans for the occasion.

sources.title: でんぶ うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
「ゆずかん」は、ゆずの皮や果肉、果汁をふんだんに使ったさっぱりとしたデザートで、ゆずゼリーとも呼ばれる。那賀町で盛んに栽培される「木頭ゆず」を使い、果汁をゼリー部分に、スライスした果肉や皮を彩りに使うことが多い。かむとゆずの爽やかな香りと酸味がふわりと広がり、暑い時季でも食べやすい後味の軽いおやつとなっている。ゆずを半分に切って中身をくり抜き、器として使うと華やかに仕上がる。
## どう作るのか
ゆずを搾って果汁を取り、ゼリー液のベースに使う。皮や果肉は薄くスライスして彩りとして加えることが多く、器としてゆずの皮を使う場合は半分に切って中身を丁寧にくり抜く。ゼリー液を型や器に流し込んで冷やし固めれば完成で、家庭でおやつとして手軽に作られている。仕上げにゆずの薄切りを浮かべたり、蜂蜜を加えて甘みを調整したりと、家庭ごとに工夫を凝らすことも多いという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
那賀町一帯は降水量が多く昼夜の寒暖差が大きいことから、良質なゆずが豊富に採れる土地として知られている。ゆべしやゆず酢など加工品づくりが盛んな土地柄の中で、より手軽におやつとして楽しめる形を模索した結果、ゆずかんが生まれたと考えられる。近年はデザートとしての需要が高まり、家庭だけでなく商品としても販売されるようになっているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Yuzukan is a refreshing dessert made generously with yuzu peel, flesh, and juice, also known as yuzu jelly. It's typically made with "Kito yuzu," widely grown in Naka town, using the juice as the base of the jelly and thin slices of peel or flesh for color. A bite releases a light burst of citrus aroma and tartness, making it an easy, clean-tasting treat even in hot weather. Cutting a yuzu in half and hollowing it out to use as a cup makes for an especially festive presentation.
## How it's made
Yuzu is squeezed for its juice, which becomes the base of the jelly liquid. The peel and flesh are often thinly sliced and added for color, and when the peel is used as a serving cup, the fruit is halved and carefully hollowed out. The jelly liquid is poured into molds or cups and chilled until set — a simple treat easily made at home.
## Why it took this shape
The Naka town area is known for plentiful, high-quality yuzu thanks to heavy rainfall and a wide swing between day and night temperatures. In a region already known for processed yuzu products like yubeshi and yuzu vinegar, yuzukan appears to have emerged from a search for a simpler way to enjoy the fruit as a snack. Demand for it as a dessert is said to have grown in recent years, and it's now sold as a product as well as made at home.

sources.title: ゆずかん うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
伊勢エビの味噌汁は、ひげや脚が取れて出荷できなくなった「あがり」と呼ばれる伊勢エビを、殻ごと豪快に使う美波町の家庭料理。エビみそのコクと殻から出る濃厚なだしが味噌の風味と溶け合い、身はぷりぷりとした弾力を持つ。生きたエビを縦半分に割ってぶつ切りにし、砂袋や背わたを除いて鍋に入れるため、見た目にも迫力がある一品となっている。玉ねぎやわかめを加え、白みそで仕立てることが多いが、赤みそや合わせみそを使う家庭もあるという。
## どう作るのか
伊勢エビは水の状態から鍋に入れてじっくり煮出し、殻や頭からしっかりとだしを取る。ある程度火が通ったらみそを溶き入れてひと煮立ちさせ、仕上げにねぎを散らせば完成となる。玉ねぎやわかめを具材に加えるほか、ゆでたそば米を入れて楽しむこともあるという。身は具として味噌汁に入れるだけでなく、一部を刺身に取り分けてから残りを汁にする家庭もある。
## なぜこの形になったのか
伊勢エビは高級食材として知られるが、水深5〜20mの浅瀬を刺し網で狙う漁の性質上、ひげや脚が取れて出荷できない「あがり」が一定数出るとされる。それを捨てずに家庭で味わう知恵として根づいたのが、この味噌汁だと考えられる。漁が解禁される9月から翌年5月まで、産卵期を避けて漁が行われ、海が荒れる時季ほど多く取れるといい、旬の恵みを余さず食べ尽くす発想から生まれた料理といえそうだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
This miso soup from Minami town is a home-style dish that puts to full use "agari" — Japanese spiny lobsters that have lost an antenna or leg during the catch and can't be sold whole. The rich flavor of the lobster's roe and shell dissolves into the broth alongside the miso, and the meat stays firm and springy. Live lobsters are split lengthwise and cut into chunks, with the sand sac and vein removed before going into the pot, making for a dramatic-looking dish. Onion and wakame seaweed are common additions, and while white miso is typical, some households use red or mixed miso instead.
## How it's made
The lobster goes into the pot with cold water and is simmered slowly so the shell and head release their full flavor into the broth. Once it's mostly cooked through, miso is stirred in and the soup is brought back to a boil, finished with a scattering of scallions. Onion and wakame are common additions, and some cooks stir in boiled sobagome (buckwheat groats) as well. Rather than using all the meat in the soup, some households set part of it aside as sashimi and use only the rest in the broth.
## Why it took this shape
Japanese spiny lobster is generally known as a premium ingredient, but the gill-net method used to catch it in the shallow waters five to twenty meters deep reportedly produces a certain number of "agari" — lobsters missing an antenna or leg that can't be sold whole. This soup appears to have taken root as a way for households to enjoy that catch rather than waste it. The season runs from September, when it reopens, through the following May, avoiding the lobsters' spawning period, and catches are said to be larger when the sea is rough — a dish that seems to have grown out of using the season's bounty to the fullest.

sources.title: 伊勢エビの味噌汁 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
蒸したさつまいもにもち粉を加えてこねた生地であずき餡を包む、素朴な餅菓子。さつまいものほくほくとした甘みともち粉のもちもちとした食感が重なり、仕上げにまぶすきな粉の香ばしさがアクセントになる。徳島は鳴門市周辺を中心にさつまいも栽培が盛んで、穏やかな気候とミネラル分の多い土壌がさつまいもづくりに向くとされる。19世紀後半にさつまいもが伝わって以降、砂糖が貴重だった時代にも比較的手に入りやすい甘みとして親しまれてきたという。
## どう作るのか
皮をむいたさつまいもをゆでるか蒸すかしてやわらかくし、もち粉、砂糖、塩、湯を加えてペースト状になるまで練り上げる。50gほどに分けてあんを包み、丸めてきな粉をまぶせば完成となる。さつまいもは切ってから時間が経つと変色しやすいため、皮をむいたら水にさらしておくのがポイントとされ、これによって鮮やかな黄色に仕上がる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
かつて砂糖などの甘いものは高級品で、一般家庭には手が届きにくかったとされる。一方でさつまいもは甘みがあり比較的入手しやすく、満腹感も得られたことから、貴重な砂糖の代わりとして重宝されたと伝わる。秋の収穫を祝う「お亥の子さん」では「お亥の子餅」として作られ、正月の餅つきでも生いもをもち米とともに突き込む家庭があったという。稲刈りや芋の収穫後のおやつとしても親しまれてきたようだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Imomochi wraps sweet red bean paste in a dough made from steamed sweet potato kneaded with glutinous rice flour — a simple confection. The mealy sweetness of the potato meets the chewy texture of the rice flour, and a dusting of roasted soybean flour on top adds a nutty finish. Tokushima grows a lot of sweet potato, especially around Naruto, where a mild climate and mineral-rich soil are said to suit the crop. Sweet potatoes reportedly arrived in the region in the late 19th century, and because they offered sweetness that was comparatively easy to come by even when sugar was scarce, they are said to have become a favorite ever since.
## How it's made
Peeled sweet potato is boiled or steamed until soft, then kneaded with glutinous rice flour, sugar, salt, and hot water into a smooth paste. It's divided into roughly 50-gram portions, wrapped around sweet bean paste, rolled into balls, and dusted with roasted soybean flour. Since cut sweet potato discolors quickly, keeping it submerged in water right after peeling is said to be the key step, which is what keeps the finished dough a bright yellow.
## Why it took this shape
Sugar and other sweets were once considered luxuries out of reach for most households, it's said. Sweet potatoes, by contrast, were naturally sweet, relatively easy to obtain, and filling, and are said to have been valued as a stand-in for scarce sugar. At the autumn harvest festival "O-ino-ko-san," the dish was reportedly made as "o-ino-ko mochi," and some households pounded raw sweet potato together with glutinous rice at New Year's mochi-making. It also seems to have been enjoyed as a snack after rice or sweet potato harvests.

sources.title: いももち うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
一般的なそうめんはめんつゆで食べるが、牟岐町の島そうめんは出羽島で取れるれんこ鯛の甘辛い煮汁をつゆ代わりに使うのが特徴。魚の旨みが染み出した煮汁にそうめんをくぐらせると、魚のうまみとしょうゆ、みりんの甘辛さがそうめんに絡み、錦糸卵やかまぼこ、ねぎの彩りが華やかさを添える。れんこ鯛の身も一緒に味わえるため、めん料理でありながらごちそう感のある一皿になっている。
## どう作るのか
れんこ鯛はうろこと内臓を取り除き、しょうゆ、みりん、砂糖などでしっかりと煮込んで甘辛い煮汁を作る。そうめんは別にゆでて冷水で洗い、器に盛った上から煮汁をかけ、錦糸卵やかまぼこ、ねぎなどを彩りよく散らして仕上げる。好みですりおろししょうがを添えるとさっぱりとした後味になるという。煮魚とそうめんを一緒に味わえる、無駄のない仕立て方になっている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
島そうめんは、祭りや婚礼、宴会など祝いの席でれんこ鯛の煮付けとともに供されてきたとされる。ごちそうとして魚を煮付けた後、残った煮汁を無駄にせずそうめんのつゆとして活用したことが始まりと考えられ、祝いの魚料理と日常のめん料理を組み合わせた合理的な工夫といえそうだ。出羽島でのアートイベントなどでも振る舞われることがあるという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
While somen noodles are usually eaten with a dashi-based dipping sauce, Mugi town's shima somen instead uses the sweet-savory braising liquid from renko-dai (a type of sea bream) caught around Deba island. Dipping the noodles in the fish-infused broth coats them in the umami of the fish along with the sweetness and salt of soy sauce and mirin, while shredded egg crepe, fish cake, and scallions add color. Since the fish itself is served alongside, this noodle dish carries the heft of a proper feast.
## How it's made
The renko-dai is scaled and gutted, then simmered thoroughly in soy sauce, mirin, and sugar to make a sweet-savory braising liquid. The somen is boiled separately, rinsed in cold water, plated, and topped with the braising liquid along with colorful garnishes of shredded egg crepe, fish cake, and scallions. Grated ginger is sometimes added for a cleaner finish. Serving the braised fish and the noodles together makes for an efficient way to use every part of the dish.
## Why it took this shape
Shima somen is said to have been served alongside braised renko-dai at festivals, weddings, and banquets — occasions calling for a proper feast. It appears to have begun as a way of not wasting the braising liquid left over after cooking the fish for a celebration, repurposing it as a noodle sauce — a practical pairing of a festive fish dish with an everyday noodle one. It's also reportedly served at art events held on Deba island.

sources.title: 島そうめん うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
一般的にかぼちゃで作られることが多い「いとこ煮」を、徳島ではゆで干しにしたさつまいもと小豆で仕立てる。干すことでうま味と甘みが凝縮された芋のねっとりとした食感に、小豆のほっくりとした食感とやさしい甘さが重なり、素朴で滋味深い味わいになる。干し芋には生のまま干す「白干し」と、一度ゆでてから干す「ゆで干し」があり、阿波のいとこ煮ではゆで干しを用いるという。
## どう作るのか
ゆで干しした干し芋を水で戻し、小豆と塩少々とともに鍋に入れて弱火で2時間ほど炊き上げる。干し芋は煮えるまで時間がかかるため、小豆をあらかじめ別に煮ておき、後から合わせるのがコツとされる。芋の切り方やゆで加減、小豆の分量は家庭によって異なり、それぞれに個性が出る仕上がりになるという。保存がきくことから、大きな鍋にまとめて作る家庭が多かったと伝わる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
冬になると空気が乾燥し、干し柿や切り干し大根、干し芋といった乾物づくりが盛んになる土地柄が背景にあるとされる。多くの家庭が芋を畑で育てていたことから、保存の知恵として干し芋にする習慣が根づき、それを使う料理として阿波のいとこ煮が生まれたと考えられる。ハレの日の食材であった小豆を用いることから、体と心を温める寒い時季の料理として親しまれてきたという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Itoko-ni is usually made with kabocha squash, but the Awa version from Tokushima uses sun-dried sweet potato and azuki beans instead. Drying concentrates the potato's umami and sweetness into a dense, sticky texture, which pairs with the mealy bite and gentle sweetness of the beans for a simple, deeply comforting flavor. There are two ways to dry the potato — "shiroboshi," dried raw, and "yudeboshi," boiled first and then dried — and the Awa version is said to use the boiled-and-dried kind.
## How it's made
The boiled-and-dried sweet potato is rehydrated in water, then simmered with azuki beans and a pinch of salt over low heat for about two hours. Because the dried potato takes a long time to soften, boiling the beans separately beforehand and combining them later is said to be the trick. How the potato is cut, how soft it's boiled, and how much bean is used all vary by household, giving each version its own character. Since it keeps well, it was reportedly common to make a large potful at once.
## Why it took this shape
The dry winter air in the region is said to have long encouraged making dried foods like persimmons, daikon strips, and sweet potato. With many households growing their own potatoes, drying them for storage became an established practice, and this dish appears to have grown out of putting that dried potato to use. Because azuki beans were once reserved for special occasions, the dish is said to have become a cold-weather favorite valued for warming both body and spirit.

sources.title: 阿波のいとこ煮 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
鳴門海峡の渦潮にもまれて育つ「鳴門鯛」を丸ごと、あるいはぶつ切りにして米とともに炊き上げる鯛めし。渦潮の中で泳ぎ育つことで身が引き締まり、うま味の強い鯛に仕上がるとされる。炊き上がったご飯には鯛の脂と旨みがしっかりと染み込み、ふっくらとした身のほぐし加減とだしの効いたご飯の組み合わせが評判の一皿になっている。
## どう作るのか
徳島の鯛めしは、洗った米の上に焼いた鯛をのせて一緒に炊き上げ、炊き上がった後に骨や皮を取り除いてご飯に混ぜ込むのが基本の作り方とされる。他県では切り身をそのまま炊き込んだり、漬けにした生の切り身を炊きたてのご飯にのせたりする方法も見られるが、焼いてから炊き込む徳島の手法は、香ばしさと旨みをより強く引き出す狙いがあるようだ。
## なぜこの形になったのか
鳴門海峡の激しい渦潮にもまれて育つ鳴門鯛は身が締まり、刺身でも珍重される食材とされる。その鯛を余さず味わう調理法として、丸ごと米と炊き込む鯛めしが発展したと考えられる。家庭で作られることは少なく、基本的には飲食店で通年提供される料理とされ、観光客が徳島を訪れた際に味わう名物としても親しまれてきたようだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Taimeshi is made by cooking a whole or roughly cut sea bream — Naruto's tai, raised amid the churning whirlpools of the Naruto Strait — together with rice. Growing up in that turbulent current is said to firm up the fish's flesh and concentrate its flavor. As the rice cooks, it soaks up the fish's fat and umami, and the combination of tender, flaked fish and richly flavored rice is what the dish is known for.
## How it's made
In the Tokushima style, a grilled sea bream is placed on top of washed rice and cooked together, and once done, the bones and skin are removed and the meat is mixed through the rice — said to be the standard method here. Elsewhere in Japan, fillets are sometimes cooked into the rice directly, or raw marinated fillets are laid over freshly cooked rice instead, but grilling the fish first, as is done in Tokushima, appears aimed at drawing out more aroma and flavor.
## Why it took this shape
Naruto tai, raised amid the strait's powerful whirlpools, is said to develop firm flesh prized even for sashimi. Cooking the whole fish into rice looks like a method that developed to make full use of that fish without waste. It's said to be rarely made at home and instead served mainly at restaurants year-round, having become a local specialty visitors are said to enjoy when they come to Tokushima.

sources.title: 鯛めし うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
煮干しと昆布のだしに白みそを溶き入れた、彩り豊かな雑煮。だいこん、にんじん、さといも、小松菜などの野菜をふんだんに使い、餅やかまぼこも加えるため、見た目も具だくさんで華やかになる。白みその甘みとやさしいコクに根菜の甘みが重なり、口当たりのまろやかな一杯に仕上がる。勝浦では黒砂糖を、相生地区では砂糖を加えて甘みを強める家庭もあるという。
## どう作るのか
煮干しと昆布でだしを取り、だいこんやにんじん、さといもといった火の通りにくい根菜から先に入れてやわらかく煮込む。生しいたけやかまぼこなどやわらかい具材を加えてから白みそを溶き入れ、仕上げに小松菜などの青菜を添える。餅は焼いてから加える家庭とゆでて加える家庭があるといい、だいこんを亀甲切り、にんじんを梅型にするなど、縁起の良い形に整えることもあるとされる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
徳島の雑煮は地域ごとに個性が強く、祖谷地方の「うちがえ雑煮」がしょうゆ仕立てで岩豆腐を使うのに対し、白味噌雑煮は白みそとすまし以外の仕立てで青菜をふんだんに使うのが特徴とされる。かつては12月から3月に採れる「まな」というアブラナ科の青菜を使うのが一般的だったが、まなが手に入りにくくなった近年は小松菜や春菊、水菜などで代用する家庭が増えているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Shiromiso zōni is a colorful New Year's soup made by dissolving white miso into a dashi of dried sardines and kelp. It's loaded with vegetables like daikon, carrot, taro, and komatsuna greens, along with rice cakes and fish cake, making for a hearty, visually vivid bowl. The sweetness and gentle richness of the white miso meet the natural sweetness of the root vegetables for a mellow, rounded flavor. Some households in Katsuura add brown sugar, and some in the Aioi district add white sugar, for extra sweetness.
## How it's made
Dashi is made from dried sardines and kelp, and slow-cooking root vegetables like daikon, carrot, and taro go in first to soften. Softer ingredients such as fresh shiitake and fish cake are added next, followed by the white miso stirred in to dissolve, and the dish is finished with a scattering of komatsuna or other greens. Some households grill the rice cakes before adding them, others boil them, and daikon is sometimes cut into a hexagonal "tortoise shell" shape or carrot punched into plum blossoms for a festive touch.
## Why it took this shape
Zōni varies widely from one part of Tokushima to another — the "uchigae zōni" of the Iya region, for instance, is soy-based and uses rock tofu instead of rice cakes — and shiromiso zōni is distinguished by its white-miso base and its generous use of leafy greens. It's said that "mana," a brassica green harvested from December through March, was traditionally used, but as mana has become harder to find in recent years, more households are said to be substituting komatsuna, shungiku, or mizuna instead.

sources.title: 白味噌雑煮 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
そば米雑炊とご飯を別々に炊いて重ね、混ぜて食べる県西部の郷土料理。ご飯をそば米で「包む」ことからこの名がついたとされ、鶏肉、油揚げ、にんじん、大根、ちくわなどの具を煮込んだそば米雑炊のとろみとだしの旨みが、炊きたてのご飯にじんわりと染み込む。そば米ならではのぷちぷちとした食感と、ご飯のふっくらとした食感が一緒に楽しめる一皿になっている。
## どう作るのか
そば米雑炊とご飯をそれぞれ別に炊き上げ、器に盛ったご飯の上からそば米雑炊をのせて混ぜ合わせて食べる。具材や作り方はどの家庭もほぼ同じで、大きな違いは見られないという。同じ具材を米と一緒に炊き込んでしまうと「包飯」とは呼ばず、あくまでも雑炊とご飯を別々に用意して重ねる作り方が、この料理の決め手になっている。
## なぜこの形になったのか
米が少なかった農村部の徳島では、そばの実やそば米で米をかさ増しする工夫が広く見られたとされる。包飯もその流れの中で、祖谷地方のそば米雑炊が里へ伝わり、ご飯と組み合わせる形へ変化していったと考えられる。ただ、そば米雑炊は今も家庭で作られ続けている一方、包飯そのものは若い世代にあまり浸透しておらず、作る家庭は少なくなっているという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Tsutsumi-meshi is a western Tokushima dish in which sobagome zōsui (buckwheat groat porridge) and plain rice are cooked separately, then layered and mixed together. The name is said to come from the idea of "wrapping" the rice in the buckwheat groats. The starchy warmth and dashi-rich flavor of the zōsui — simmered with chicken, fried tofu, carrot, daikon, and fish cake — soaks gradually into the freshly cooked rice, so a single bowl carries both the light snap of the groats and the softness of the rice.
## How it's made
The sobagome zōsui and the plain rice are each cooked on their own, then the rice is plated and the zōsui is ladled over it and mixed together before eating. The ingredients and method are said to be much the same from one household to the next, with little variation. Cooking the same ingredients together with the rice from the start isn't called tsutsumi-meshi; keeping the porridge and the rice separate until they are combined at the table is what defines the dish.
## Why it took this shape
In the farming communities of rural Tokushima, where rice was once scarce, stretching it with buckwheat groats or whole buckwheat was reportedly a common workaround. Tsutsumi-meshi appears to have grown out of that same tradition, evolving as sobagome zōsui from the Iya mountains spread down to the lowland villages and was paired with rice. Sobagome zōsui itself is still commonly made at home today, but tsutsumi-meshi has not caught on with younger generations, and fewer households are said to make it now.

sources.title: 包飯 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
里芋の一種、ヤツガシラの葉柄にあたる「ずいき」を、ゆでてから合わせ酢で和えた一品。生のずいきは薄紫色をしているが、ゆでると一度黒っぽく変わり、酢で和えると鮮やかな赤色に変化するのが特徴で、食卓を彩る料理として親しまれてきたという。ほどよくゆでるとしゃきしゃきとした歯ごたえが残り、砂糖やしょうゆ、徳島特産のゆずを使った柚子酢を合わせた甘酸っぱい味わいになる。
## どう作るのか
ずいきは皮をむいて5cmほどに切り、酢水に浸けてあくを抜いてからゆでる。油抜きして細切りにした油揚げと合わせ、砂糖やしょうゆ、柚子酢などで作った合わせ酢で和える。ゆでずに炒めてから使う家庭や、干しずいきを戻して使う家庭もあるという。ずいきに触れると手がかゆくなることがあるため、あらかじめ酢で手を濡らしてから調理するのがコツとされる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
ずきがしが食卓に並ぶようになったのは、砂糖が一般家庭でも使いやすくなってからとされる。芋の収穫前にあたる夏場によく食べられていたといい、里芋を育てる過程で出るずいきを余さず使い切る知恵から生まれた料理と考えられる。すだちの皮をすりおろして風味を添える家庭もあったといい、旬の柑橘とともに夏らしいさっぱりとした一皿として親しまれてきたようだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Zukigashi dresses boiled zuiki — the petiole of the yatsugashira taro plant — in a sweet-tart vinegar sauce. Raw zuiki has a pale purple color that turns almost black once boiled, then shifts to a vivid red once tossed in vinegar, making the dish a striking addition to the table. Boiled just enough, it keeps a crisp, crunchy bite, and the dressing — a mix of sugar, soy sauce, and yuzu vinegar made from Tokushima's local citrus — gives it a sweet and tangy flavor.
## How it's made
The zuiki is peeled, cut into roughly five-centimeter lengths, soaked in vinegar water to remove bitterness, and then boiled. It's combined with thinly sliced fried tofu that has had its oil rinsed off, and dressed in a vinegar mix of sugar, soy sauce, and yuzu vinegar. Some households sauté the zuiki instead of boiling it, or rehydrate dried zuiki rather than using it fresh. Since handling raw zuiki can make the skin itch, wetting the hands with vinegar beforehand is said to be a useful trick.
## Why it took this shape
Zukigashi is said to have appeared on tables once sugar became easier for ordinary households to use. It was commonly eaten in summer, before the taro harvest, and appears to have developed as a way of making full use of the zuiki that comes off the plant while growing the taro itself, rather than letting it go to waste. Some households add grated sudachi peel for extra fragrance, making it a refreshing dish tied to the season's citrus.

sources.title: ずきがし うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
鮎を一尾丸ごと使った雑炊「鮎ろうすい」。「ろうすい」は雑炊がなまった呼び名とされ、じゃがいもやたまねぎ、なすなどの夏野菜とご飯を鮎のだしで煮込み、みそで味を調える。鮎の風味が汁全体に行き渡り、川魚らしい香りと野菜の甘みが溶け合った滋味深い味わいになる。勝浦川で育つ鮎は苔を食べて育つため腹の部分まで食べられ、内臓ごと加えて独特の風味を楽しむのが一般的だという。
## どう作るのか
鮎はうろこを取り除き、炊いた米やじゃがいも、たまねぎなど火の通りにくい野菜と一緒にだし汁で煮込む。具材がやわらかくなったら、なすやしめじ、にらなどやわらかい野菜を加えてみそを溶き入れ、仕上げにすだちの薄切りを添える。内臓が苦手な場合は取り除いて作ることもあるという。清流として知られる勝浦川で取れたての鮎を使うのが本来の作り方とされる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
勝浦川は鮎やあめご、うなぎ、鯉など川魚の宝庫として知られ、6月の鮎釣り解禁とともに旬を迎える。瀬張り網漁でとれた鮎を、夏野菜とともにその場で雑炊に仕立てて食べていたことがこの料理の始まりと考えられる。水産資源を守るため10月下旬から翌年5月頃までは禁漁とする期間があるとされ、限られた旬の恵みを丸ごと味わい尽くす発想から生まれた料理といえそうだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Ayu rōsui is a rice porridge built around a whole sweetfish, its name said to be a slurred form of "zōsui" (rice porridge). Potato, onion, eggplant, and other summer vegetables are simmered with rice in a dashi made from the fish, then seasoned with miso. The sweetfish's flavor runs through the whole pot, giving the dish the aroma of river fish balanced against the sweetness of the vegetables. Sweetfish from the Katsuura River are said to feed on algae, which makes even their innards edible, and they are typically added whole, guts included, for their distinctive flavor.
## How it's made
The sweetfish is scaled and simmered in dashi together with cooked rice and firmer vegetables like potato and onion. Once those soften, more delicate vegetables such as eggplant, shimeji mushrooms, and garlic chives go in, followed by miso stirred in to season the broth, and the dish is finished with thin slices of sudachi. The innards are sometimes removed for those who prefer it that way. Using freshly caught sweetfish from the clear Katsuura River is said to be the traditional approach.
## Why it took this shape
The Katsuura River is known for sweetfish, amego trout, eel, and carp, and the sweetfish season opens with the start of ayu fishing in June. The dish appears to have begun as a way of turning fish caught with shallow-water gill nets into a porridge on the spot, together with summer vegetables. A closed season from late October through around May the following year is said to protect the fish population, and the dish looks like a way of making the most of that limited seasonal catch.

sources.title: 鮎ろうすい うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
平らな石を「ひらら」と呼び、その石を熱してあめごや山菜、豆腐、こんにゃくなどをみそとともに焼き上げる、三好市祖谷地域の野外料理。じっくりと熱を通した石の上で、あめごの香ばしさとみその風味、豆腐やこんにゃくのやさしい味わいが混ざり合う。石豆腐（岩豆腐）など祖谷ならではの食材を使うのも特徴で、野趣あふれる仕上がりになる。
## どう作るのか
かまどの上に平らな石を置いて熱し、みそで丸く土手を作ったところに水や砂糖、酒を加えて3時間ほどじっくり火を通す。石が十分に温まったら、あめごや山菜、こんにゃく、豆腐などをのせて焼き上げる。現在ではホットプレートに調味料を混ぜて敷き、あめごに加えて鶏肉やじゃがいも、生しいたけなど好みの具材を焼く簡易的な作り方も広まっているという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
石を温めるには数時間かかるとされ、その間に山であめごや山菜を採ってくるという段取りから、自然と野外での共同作業を伴う料理として根づいたと考えられる。近隣の村との交流や、家族・友人が集まる際のもてなし料理として供されてきたとされ、次第に山遊びの折に楽しむ野外料理としても親しまれるようになったという。険しい山あいで暮らしてきた祖谷地域ならではの、身近な自然の恵みと時間を分かち合う知恵が形になった料理といえそうだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Hirarayaki takes its name from "hirara," a flat stone, which is heated and used to grill amego trout, mountain vegetables, tofu, and konjac together with miso — an outdoor dish from the Iya region of Miyoshi. The slow heat of the stone brings out the amego's aroma alongside the flavor of the miso and the gentle taste of the tofu and konjac. Local specialties like rock tofu (iwa-dōfu) round out the ingredients, giving the dish a rustic, wild character.
## How it's made
A flat stone is set over a hearth and heated, and a ring of miso is built up on its surface to form a wall; water, sugar, and sake are poured in and simmered slowly for about three hours. Once the stone is thoroughly heated, amego, mountain vegetables, konjac, and tofu are laid on top and grilled. These days a simplified version is also common, using a hot plate spread with the seasoning mixture and topped with amego along with chicken, potato, fresh shiitake, or other vegetables to taste.
## Why it took this shape
Heating the stone was said to take several hours, and during that wait people would go gather amego and mountain vegetables, which appears to be how the dish naturally became tied to outdoor, communal preparation. It's said to have been served to guests from neighboring villages and at gatherings of family and friends, and it eventually became a favorite outdoor dish enjoyed on trips into the mountains as well.

sources.title: あめごのひらら焼き うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
黒糖と薄力粉、重曹、みょうばんで作る蒸しパンのようなお菓子。中に空洞ができる様子を徳島の方言で「ほた」と呼ぶことが名前の由来とされる。黒糖を使うため濃い茶色に仕上がり、もっちりとした食感とコクのある素朴な甘みが特徴。大正時代までは「松風」と呼ばれる蒸しようかんが親しまれ、昭和初期に駄菓子屋で売られるようになってから「ほたようかん」の名で広まったという。
## どう作るのか
黒糖に適量の重曹を加え、甘くふっくらと仕上げるのがコツとされる。重曹を入れすぎると苦みが出やすく、逆に黒糖をしっかり溶かさないと生地にぼつぼつと黒い穴があいてしまうため、加減が難しいという。生地を型に流し込んで蒸し上げれば完成となる。精製されていない黒砂糖は安価で扱いやすく、コクのある甘さを出しやすいことから広く使われてきたとされる。
## なぜこの形になったのか
ほたようかんは、農作業の合間の休憩に食べる軽食として広まったとされ、疲れた体をいたわる甘みとして重宝されてきたという。豊作を祝う際にも作られていたと伝わり、多めに仕込んで近所にお裾分けする習わしもあったとされる。黒砂糖という比較的手に入りやすい甘味料を使い、家庭で手軽に作れる蒸し菓子として根づいたことが、今も広く親しまれている理由のようだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Hotayōkan is a steamed cake-like sweet made from brown sugar, soft wheat flour, baking soda, and alum. Its name comes from "hota," a local dialect word for the hollow that forms inside as it steams. The brown sugar gives it a deep brown color, a chewy texture, and a rich, simple sweetness. Before the Taisho era, a similar steamed confection called "matsukaze" was eaten instead, and it is said to have taken on the name "hotayōkan" once it began being sold at candy shops in the early Showa era.
## How it's made
Getting the right amount of baking soda into the brown sugar batter is said to be the key to a light, sweet finish — too much and it turns bitter, while not fully dissolving the brown sugar leaves dark pockmarks in the batter, so the balance takes some care. The batter is poured into a mold and steamed until set. Unrefined brown sugar was inexpensive and easy to work with, and its deep sweetness is said to be why it became the sugar of choice for this cake.
## Why it took this shape
Hotayōkan is said to have spread as a snack eaten during breaks from farm work, its sweetness valued as a comfort for tired bodies. It's also said to have been made to celebrate a good harvest, with households making extra to share with neighbors. Built around brown sugar, a relatively accessible sweetener, and simple enough to make at home, it appears to have taken root as an everyday steamed treat, which seems to be why it's still so well loved today.

sources.title: ほたようかん うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
一口大の「ごうしゅいも」というじゃがいもや、そば粉を練った団子、岩豆腐、丸こんにゃくを串に刺し、みそだれを塗って焼く三好市祖谷地方の郷土料理。素焼きにした具材にみその香ばしさが加わり、ごうしゅいものほくほくとした食感、そば団子のもっちり感、岩豆腐や丸こんにゃくの弾力ある歯ごたえが一本の串で味わえる。串を回しながら焼く姿が、阿波人形浄瑠璃の木偶人形が頭を回す様子に似ていることが名の由来とされる。
## どう作るのか
ごうしゅいもとこんにゃくをゆでて下ごしらえし、そば粉は水で練って丸め、ゆでて団子にする。これらと一口大に切った岩豆腐を竹串に刺し、囲炉裏で一度素焼きにしてから、みそだれを塗ってさらに焼き上げる。串をぐるぐると回しながら満遍なく火を通すのが特徴で、具材は上からごうしゅいも、豆腐、こんにゃくの順に刺し、滑りにくいこんにゃくが上の具材を支える役割を果たすという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
祖谷地方では小ぶりのごうしゅいもや、岩のように硬い岩豆腐、そば粉といった特産品が豊富に取れることから、これらを一本の串にまとめて味わう料理として発展したと考えられる。囲炉裏を囲んで串を回しながら焼く工程は、山あいの暮らしの中で家族や仲間と火を囲む時間そのものを料理に取り込んだものといえそうだ。ごうしゅいもの収穫が多い時期には、いもだけで作ることもあったという。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Decomawashi skewers bite-sized "gōshu-imo" potatoes, dumplings made from kneaded buckwheat flour, rock tofu, and round pieces of konjac, then grills them brushed with a miso glaze — a dish from the Iya region of Miyoshi. The plain-grilled skewer picks up the aroma of the miso, and a single stick carries the mealy bite of the potato, the chewiness of the buckwheat dumpling, and the springy texture of the tofu and konjac together. The way the skewer is turned while grilling is said to resemble the head-turning motion of a deku puppet from Awa puppet theater, reportedly the source of the dish's name.
## How it's made
The gōshu-imo potatoes and konjac are boiled first, and buckwheat flour is kneaded with water, rolled into balls, and boiled into dumplings. These, along with bite-sized pieces of rock tofu, are skewered on bamboo sticks, grilled plain over an open hearth, then brushed with a miso glaze and grilled further. The skewer is turned continuously so everything cooks evenly, and the ingredients are typically threaded in the order of potato, tofu, then konjac from the top, with the less slippery konjac said to help hold the other pieces in place.
## Why it took this shape
The Iya region is rich in small gōshu-imo potatoes, stone-hard rock tofu, and buckwheat flour, and the dish appears to have developed as a way to bring all of these local specialties together on a single skewer. Grilling the skewers while gathered around a hearth looks like a way mountain communities built their shared fireside time into the cooking process itself. In seasons when the potato harvest was especially plentiful, it's said the skewers were sometimes made with potato alone.

sources.title: 祖谷のでこまわし うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
里芋の一種「はすいも」の茎と太刀魚を、しょうゆや酢、砂糖を合わせた酢で和えた県南部の郷土料理。はすいもの茎はしゃきしゃきとした歯切れの良い食感が持ち味で、太刀魚のほのかな甘みと合わせ酢の酸味が加わり、さっぱりとした後味に仕上がる。はすいもは東南アジア原産とされ、沖縄経由で伝わったことから「りゅうきゅう」とも呼ばれるという。県西部でよく食べられる「ずいき」と似ているが、こちらは里芋の葉柄で、はすいもとは別の部位を指す。
## どう作るのか
皮をむいたはすいもの茎を食べやすい長さに切り、食べやすく切った太刀魚を酢に漬けておく。しょうゆ、酢、砂糖を合わせた酢に両方を加えて和え、仕上げにみょうがを添えれば完成となる。油揚げやちりめんじゃこ、ツナ缶、大葉などを加えるとさらに風味豊かになるという。太刀魚の皮が苦手な場合は、あらかじめ取り除いてから作ることもある。
## なぜこの形になったのか
はすいもの旬は7月から9月、太刀魚も夏から秋にかけて旬を迎えることから、両者を組み合わせた酢の物は暑い時季に食欲をそそる一品として親しまれてきたとされる。県南部の沿岸で太刀魚が身近な魚であったことと、温暖な気候で育ちやすいはすいもが庭先などで栽培されていたことが結びつき、日常のおかずとして定着したと考えられる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
This dish from southern Tokushima dresses the stems of "hasuimo" — a relative of taro — together with cutlassfish in a vinegar sauce of soy sauce, vinegar, and sugar. The hasuimo stems have a crisp, snappy bite, and the fish's mild sweetness combines with the vinegar's tartness for a refreshing finish. Hasuimo is said to originate in Southeast Asia and to have reached Tokushima by way of Okinawa, where it's also known as "ryūkyū." It resembles "zuiki," a taro-stem vegetable eaten more often in western Tokushima, but the two come from different parts of the plant.
## How it's made
The peeled hasuimo stems are cut into easy-to-eat lengths, and the cutlassfish, also cut into pieces, is marinated in vinegar. Both are then tossed in a vinegar dressing of soy sauce, vinegar, and sugar, and finished with a garnish of myoga ginger. Fried tofu, dried baby sardines, canned tuna, or shiso leaves are sometimes added for extra flavor. If the fish's skin isn't to someone's taste, it's sometimes removed before cooking.
## Why it took this shape
Hasuimo is in season from July to September, and cutlassfish from summer into autumn, so pairing the two in a vinegared dish is said to have become a way of stimulating appetite in the hot months. Cutlassfish being a familiar catch along the southern coast, combined with hasuimo's ease of growing in the region's mild climate — often right in home gardens — appears to be why the pairing settled in as an everyday side dish.

sources.title: はすいもの茎の酢の物 うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
蒸したさといもやさつまいもを円柱形に整え、こしあんで巻いて輪切りにした、海陽町を中心とする県南部の郷土料理。おはぎに似た見た目だが、米の代わりに芋を使うのが特徴で、ねっとりとした芋の食感とこしあんの上品な甘さが溶け合う。米が不足していた時代、芋が米の代わりとして食べられ「出世した」とみなされたことから、この縁起の良い名がついたと伝わる。現在はさといもよりもさつまいもを使うのが一般的だという。
## どう作るのか
水に浸けた小豆をゆでてミキサーでつぶし、砂糖と塩を加えてこしあんを作る。ゆでたさつまいもは皮をむいて形を整え、のばしたこしあんで巻いて冷蔵庫で冷やす。供する際は3cmほどの長さに輪切りにすると、断面にきれいな渦模様が現れる。現在は市販のあんを使って手軽に作る家庭も多いといい、さといもとさつまいもを組み合わせて作ることもあるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
米が不足していた時代、海陽町を含む県南部では米の代わりに芋類を食べる機会が多く、出世いもはそうした芋料理の一つとして考え出されたと考えられる。おはぎの代わりに作られていたといい、「出世」という縁起の良い名前から、男の子の誕生や端午の節句、結婚式など祝い事の席で供されるようになったとされる。米の代わりの芋が「出世した」という見立ては、質素な材料しかない中でも祝いの席を彩ろうとした工夫の表れといえそうだ。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Shusse-imo shapes steamed taro or sweet potato into a cylinder, wraps it in smooth red bean paste, and slices it into rounds — a dish from Kaiyō town and the surrounding area of southern Tokushima. It looks something like ohagi, but uses potato in place of rice, and the sticky texture of the potato meets the refined sweetness of the bean paste. In times when rice was scarce, potato reportedly stood in for it and was said to have been "promoted" ("shusse"), which is said to be the origin of this auspicious name. Sweet potato is more commonly used today than taro.
## How it's made
Azuki beans soaked in water are boiled, blended, and mixed with sugar and salt to make smooth red bean paste. Boiled sweet potato is peeled, shaped, wrapped in a sheet of the bean paste, and chilled in the refrigerator. Sliced into rounds about three centimeters long, each piece reveals a neat spiral cross-section. Many households today use store-bought bean paste for convenience, and some combine taro with sweet potato instead of using either alone.
## Why it took this shape
When rice was scarce, households in Kaiyō town and the rest of southern Tokushima often ate potato in its place, and shusse-imo appears to be one of the potato dishes devised in that context. It's said to have been made in place of ohagi, and thanks to its name's association with advancement in life, it came to be served at celebrations such as the birth of a son, the Boys' Festival, and sometimes even weddings. Casting a humble potato standing in for rice as something "promoted" looks like an effort to bring a festive touch to a table with modest ingredients.

sources.title: 出世いも うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
小豆のこしあんに上新粉やもち粉、砂糖を加えて蒸し上げる、徳島に伝わるういろう。もちもちとした食感に、和三盆特有の上品でやさしい甘さが重なる。江戸時代、阿波でサトウキビの栽培が広まり「阿波和三盆」が作られるようになった際、その完成を祝って作られたのが始まりと伝わる。形は四角いようかん状から丸いまんじゅう状までさまざまで、近年は栗や柿、チョコレート風味など季節や好みに合わせたアレンジも増えているという。
## どう作るのか
和三盆や砂糖、塩を混ぜ合わせて生あんに加え、上新粉やもち粉を加えてよく練る。ほどよい硬さになったら型に流し込み、気泡が残らないよう全体を揺すってから蒸し上げる。蒸し上がったら一晩寝かせて味をなじませ、食べる際に切り分けて供するのが一般的とされる。栗や柿を混ぜ込む場合は、生地を型に流し込む前に加えて彩りと食感を添えるという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
阿波ういろは、旧暦3月3日の節句に阿波和三盆の完成を祝って作られたのが始まりとされ、以来この日に食べる習慣が根づいたという。ひな祭りの飾りに供えられたほか、昭和の頃までは節句の日に重箱「遊山箱」へ巻きずしなどとともに詰めて山や海へ遊びに出かける風習があり、阿波ういろもその中に入れられていたと伝わる。地元産の砂糖と米粉という身近な材料の組み合わせが、行事とともに受け継がれてきた理由と考えられる。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Awa uiro is a steamed confection made by mixing smooth azuki bean paste with rice flour, glutinous rice flour, and sugar. Its texture is chewy, and the sweetness carries the refined, gentle character of wasanbon, the fine local sugar. It's said to date back to the Edo period, when sugarcane cultivation spread in Awa and "Awa wasanbon" sugar was first produced there; the confection is said to have been made to celebrate the completion of that sugar. Shapes range from square, yōkan-like blocks to round, manjū-like pieces, and modern versions with chestnut, persimmon, or chocolate flavoring have become more common in recent years.
## How it's made
Wasanbon sugar and salt are mixed into smooth bean paste, then rice flour and glutinous rice flour are added and kneaded well. Once the mixture reaches the right consistency, it's poured into a mold, shaken to remove air bubbles, and steamed. It's typically left to rest overnight afterward to let the flavor settle, then sliced before serving. When chestnut or persimmon is added, it's folded in before the batter goes into the mold, for both color and texture.
## Why it took this shape
Awa uiro is said to have first been made to celebrate the completion of Awa wasanbon sugar on the third day of the third lunar month, a seasonal festival, and the custom of eating it on that day is said to have taken hold from there. It was reportedly placed among the Hinamatsuri decorations, and until the Showa era, households are said to have packed it into "yuzanbako" lacquer boxes together with rolled sushi to take on outings to the mountains or sea on that same festival day. The pairing of locally made sugar with rice flour, both readily at hand, looks like what let the confection endure alongside the festival itself.

sources.title: 阿波ういろ うちの郷土料理

items.body_ja:
## 何でできているか
もち米とうるち米を混ぜて炊き、米粒が残る程度にすりつぶしてあんで包んだ、那賀町相生地区に伝わるおはぎのような菓子。米粒のつぶつぶとした食感が残るのが持ち味で、しっかりとすりつぶして作るなめらかな「みなごろし」とは異なる仕上がりになる。生地にヨモギを加えたり、仕上げにきな粉をまぶしたりする家庭もあるという。すりつぶし方が名前の由来で、「半分だけすりつぶす」ことから「はんごろし」と呼ばれるようになったと伝わる。
## どう作るのか
もち米にうるち米を混ぜて水に浸け、塩を加えて炊き上げる。炊き上がった米を、粒が残る程度に軽くすりつぶし、あんを包めば完成となる。あんは小豆から手作りする家庭も多いが、市販のものを使う場合もあるという。ヨモギを混ぜ込んで香りを添えたり、きな粉をまぶしたりと、家庭ごとに仕上げ方が少しずつ異なる。すりつぶす加減が強すぎるとなめらかな「みなごろし」になってしまうため、力加減の見極めが仕上がりを左右するという。
## なぜこの形になったのか
那賀町は平成17年に5つの町村が合併して生まれ、町域の大半を森林が占める山あいの地域とされる。中でも相生地区で親しまれてきた半ごろしは、来客をもてなす際によく振る舞われていたと伝わり、手に入りやすい米と小豆で作れる素朴な菓子が、もてなしの定番として根づいたと考えられる。一時期は「草もち」の名で販売されたこともあったが、地元の学生の声から元の名前が呼び戻されたという経緯も伝わっている。
items.body_en:
## What it's made of
Hangoroshi mixes glutinous and non-glutinous rice, cooks it, and mashes it only partway so grains still show, then wraps it in bean paste — an ohagi-like sweet from the Aioi district of Naka town. The partly mashed rice keeps a distinct graininess, different from the smoother "minagoroshi" version made by mashing the rice fully. Some households mix in mugwort for the dough or dust the finished piece with roasted soybean flour. The name is said to come from the mashing method itself — mashed only "halfway," or "han" — giving the dish its rather startling name.
## How it's made
Glutinous rice is mixed with non-glutinous rice, soaked in water, and cooked with a pinch of salt. Once cooked, the rice is lightly mashed, leaving some grains whole, and wrapped around bean paste to finish. Many households make the bean paste from azuki beans themselves, though store-bought paste is sometimes used. Mugwort is sometimes kneaded in for fragrance, and roasted soybean flour dusted on top, with the finish varying a little from household to household. Mash it too far and it turns into the smoother minagoroshi instead, so judging the pressure by feel is what decides the result.
## Why it took this shape
Naka town was formed in 2005 through the merger of five towns and villages and is mostly covered in forest, a mountainous area. Hangoroshi, especially cherished in the Aioi district, is said to have been served often to welcome guests, and a simple sweet made from readily available rice and azuki beans appears to have become the standard for that kind of hospitality. It was reportedly sold for a time under the name "kusamochi," but is said to have reverted to "hangoroshi" after local students asked for the original name back.
